characters.name: Foreman
characters.summary: Tries to keep the discussion orderly and fair without dominating it. Increasingly weary as the meeting becomes more chaotic, but continues to take responsibility for the process.

characters.name: 2nd Juror
characters.summary: Quiet, hesitant and initially easily led. Gradually gains confidence as he starts thinking about the evidence for himself. His question about the angle of the stab wound becomes an important turning point.

characters.name: 3rd Juror
characters.summary: Forceful, angry and absolutely convinced of the boy's guilt. Takes disagreement personally and becomes increasingly aggressive as the case unravels. His estrangement from his own son gradually emerges as the emotional reason he cannot let go.

characters.name: 4th Juror
characters.summary: Calm, rational and controlled. Regards himself as someone who follows evidence rather than emotion and remains one of the strongest advocates for guilty. Crucially, when the eyewitness evidence finally fails, he accepts the implication.

characters.name: 5th Juror
characters.summary: Sensitive about his own slum background and initially reluctant to speak. His personal experience gives him knowledge the others lack, particularly about switchblades. Becomes increasingly confident as the discussion progresses.

characters.name: 6th Juror
characters.summary: Straightforward, decent and practical. Not especially argumentative, but listens carefully and changes his mind when the evidence no longer convinces him.

characters.name: 7th Juror
characters.summary: Impatient and flippant, chiefly concerned with getting away to the match. Treats the deliberation as an inconvenience until his casual change of vote is challenged by the 11th Juror.

characters.name: 8th Juror
characters.summary: The central challenger. Calm, persistent and prepared to stand alone, but never claims to know that the boy is innocent. His purpose is to test whether the evidence really proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

characters.name: 9th Juror
characters.summary: Older, observant and thoughtful. First to recognise the courage of the 8th Juror's position and first to join him. Particularly perceptive about other people: the old witness's need for attention and, finally, the marks left by the woman's glasses.

characters.name: 10th Juror
characters.summary: Aggressive and prejudiced. His certainty about the boy is bound up with sweeping assumptions about 'people like him'. As those assumptions become explicit, the rest of the jury increasingly withdraws from him.

characters.name: 11th Juror
characters.summary: Precise, serious and strongly committed to the responsibility of being a juror. Values evidence and due process. His challenge to the 7th Juror makes clear that a not-guilty vote must be taken just as seriously as a guilty one.

characters.name: 12th Juror
characters.summary: Polished and socially confident but intellectually less certain than he initially appears. Impressed by presentation and liable to move with the argument. Eventually accepts that the eyewitness may have been mistaken.

characters.name: Judge
characters.summary: Heard only at the beginning. Establishes the stakes and the jury's responsibility: the verdict must be unanimous and a guilty verdict means death.

characters.name: Guard
characters.summary: A functional presence at the beginning and end, and when the knife is brought into the room. Represents the world outside the jury room while the twelve men deliberate.

beats.title: Eleven to one
beats.summary: The jurors arrive, settle in and reveal their assumptions. The first vote is eleven to one for guilty, and the 8th Juror insists they must talk before sending the boy to die.

beats.title: The case against him
beats.summary: The jurors lay out the prosecution case: the old man, the woman across the street, the boy's alibi, motive and record. The 3rd Juror's broken relationship with his own son also begins to surface.

beats.title: The knife
beats.summary: The murder weapon becomes the focus. The 8th Juror produces an identical knife, showing that the supposedly unique weapon may not be unique and giving the first serious challenge to the certainty of guilt.

beats.title: The secret ballot
beats.summary: The 8th Juror proposes a secret ballot and agrees to accept a guilty verdict if nobody supports him. The 9th Juror changes his vote, making it ten to two.

beats.title: Could he have heard it?
beats.summary: The old man's evidence is tested against the noise of the passing train. His motives and the meaning of the boy's shouted threat are questioned, and the 5th Juror changes his vote.

beats.title: Could he have reached the door?
beats.summary: The jurors reconstruct the old man's journey to his front door. It takes forty-two seconds rather than fifteen, and the argument culminates in the 3rd Juror threatening to kill the 8th.

beats.title: Six to six
beats.summary: Another open vote produces a six-to-six split. The 8th Juror then tests the 4th Juror's memory of a recent cinema visit, weakening the argument that the boy's failure to remember his film proves he was lying.

beats.title: The switchblade
beats.summary: The stabbing angle is reconstructed. The 5th Juror's experience with switchblades challenges the prosecution's version; the 7th Juror changes his vote and the 11th forces him to take that decision seriously.

beats.title: Nine to three
beats.summary: With the vote now nine to three for not guilty, the 10th Juror launches into a prejudiced tirade. The others reject both him and his reasoning, and the 8th identifies prejudice as an obstacle to judging the facts.

beats.title: The woman's glasses
beats.summary: The woman's eyewitness evidence becomes the strongest remaining case for guilt. Marks on her nose reveal that she wore glasses, raising doubt that she could have identified the boy from bed without them.

beats.title: Eleven to one
beats.summary: The 12th and 10th Jurors move to not guilty, and the 4th accepts that he now has reasonable doubt. The 3rd Juror is left alone and is asked to make his case again.

beats.title: It's not your boy
beats.summary: The 3rd Juror tries to revive the discarded evidence, but his feelings about his own son finally surface. He changes his vote to not guilty and the jury is ready to return its verdict.

script.speaker: Judge
script.text: Gentlemen of the jury, one man is dead. The life of another is at stake. If you believe that there is a reasonable doubt the accused is innocent, you must bring a verdict of ‘not guilty’. If there is no reasonable doubt, you must find the accused guilty. Your verdict must be unanimous. If you find the accused guilty, the death sentence is mandatory. You are faced with grave responsibility. Thank you, gentlemen.

script.speaker: Guard
script.text: All right, let’s move along, gentlemen.

script.speaker: Guard
script.text: I will be waiting outside. Knock if you need anything.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: This better be fast. I got tickets to the match tonight.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right, gentlemen. Let’s take seats.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I’ve never been on a jury before. God, those lawyers go on!

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well, I guess they’re entitled to…

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Sure they are. Everybody deserves a fair trial. That’s the system. Even for a reprobate like this.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Hey, how about getting started here?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: The kid’s no good. I mean, he’s got a record. He was in reform school and—

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Well, y’know, he was—

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I mean, this is one of those cases. You know what I mean.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Yeah.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: What was your impression of the prosecuting attorney?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: I beg your pardon?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I thought he was sharp. The way he hammered home his points, one by one. I was very impressed.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Yes, I think he did an expert job.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Okay, let’s get this show on the road.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right. We can discuss it first and then vote; that’s one way. Or we can—

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Yeah, let’s vote. Who knows, maybe we can all get home early!

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Just let’s remember we’ve got a first-degree murder charge here. If we vote ‘guilty’, we send the accused to the gallows. That’s mandatory.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I think we all know that.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Come on, let’s vote.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right. Remember, it must be unanimous. That’s the law. All those voting ‘guilty’ please raise your hands.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Nine… ten… eleven. That’s eleven for ‘guilty’. Okay. ‘Not guilty’?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Boy-oh-boy, there’s always one.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: So, what do we do now?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know. I guess we have to talk to each other.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Do you really think he’s innocent?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You sat in court and heard the same things we did. The man’s a dangerous killer.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: The man? He’s sixteen years old.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: It’s obvious he did it. I was convinced from the first day.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I agree.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Exactly! Then what do you want?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Nothing. I just want to talk.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: What’s there to talk about? Eleven men here agree.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Do you believe the boy’s story?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t know whether I believe it or not.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: So what’d you vote ‘not guilty’ for?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: There were eleven votes for ‘guilty’. It’s not easy for me to raise my hand and send a boy off to die without talking about it first.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Who says it’s easy for me?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: No one.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: I think he’s guilty. You couldn’t change my mind if you talked for a hundred years.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’m not trying to change your mind. We’re talking about somebody’s life here. We can’t decide in five minutes. Suppose we’re wrong?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Suppose we’re wrong? You can suppose anything.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Well then, suppose I’m right. What then?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: What’s the difference how long it takes? We think he’s guilty. So what?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: So, let’s take an hour. The game doesn’t start till eight o’clock.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Okay, fine, be my guest.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Well, who’s got something to say?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Look, this boy has clearly had a terrible sixteen years –

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: We don’t owe him anything. He got a fair trial. We heard the facts. You’re not going to tell me that kid’s innocent. You know how those people lie. They don’t need any real reason to kill someone. That’s the way they are. Violent!

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: It suddenly occurs to me that you must be an ignorant man.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What do you mean?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Do you think you have a monopoly on the truth?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: All right. We don’t need a whole sermon.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: If we’re going to discuss this case, let’s stick to the facts.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Right. Maybe we should go around the table.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well — I just think he’s guilty. I thought it was obvious. Nobody proved otherwise.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Nobody has to prove otherwise. The burden of proof is on the prosecution.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I’m just thinking out loud… but maybe we should explain to this gentleman why we’re right and he’s wrong.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Well, somebody saw the boy kill his father.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Exactly. Look at the evidence. The old man downstairs heard the kid shout, ‘I’m gonna kill you.’ A second later he heard a body fall. He ran to his door and saw the kid running down the stairs. He’s known him his whole life – he knows his voice and knows his face. There are facts for you.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: And the boy claimed he was at the movies, yet an hour later he couldn’t remember what film he saw or who starred in it. No one saw him going into or out of the theatre.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Yeah, and what about the woman across the street? She saw the kid stick the knife into his father. She could see directly into the window and she swore she saw him do it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Through the windows of a passing elevated train.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: With the lights out. They proved in court you could see through the train into the window.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You don’t believe the boy. How come you believe the woman? She’s one of ‘them’, too, isn’t she?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: You’re a pretty smart fellow, aren’t you?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Take it easy.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: What about the motive? We know he had an argument with his father around 7pm that evening. His father hit him twice and the boy left the house angry. Surely that speaks to motive.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: This boy has been hit all his life. I can’t see two slaps provoking him into murder.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Everyone has a breaking point. It may have been two slaps too many.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: And look at his record. Reform school at fourteen. Stole a car. Arrested for mugging. Picked up twice for trying to slash another kid with a knife. He’s real handy with switchblades.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: His father beat him regularly from the time he was five.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: So would I. A kid like that.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: It’s the kids, the way they are nowadays. Angry! Hostile! When I was his age I called my father ‘Sir’. I had respect.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Have you got any kids?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: One. He’s twenty. When he was nine he ran away from a fight. I told him, ‘I’m gonna make a man outa you or I’m gonna bust you in half trying.’ When he was sixteen, he hit me in the face. I haven’t seen him in two years. Rotten kid.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Look, we’re here to decide whether this boy is guilty of murder, not why he grew up this way. I mean, it’s no secret that children from slum backgrounds are potential menaces to society.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I’ve lived in a slum all my life.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I didn’t mean—

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I used to play in a backyard filled with garbage. Maybe it still smells on me.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Oh stop being a kid!

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: What’s that supposed to mean?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What do you think? K-I-D. Kid!

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Look, let’s stop arguing.. Why don’t you go?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You wanted to convince me. I’m listening.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: All right. What about the switchblade they found in the father’s chest? The one that fine, upright boy admitted buying on the night of the murder.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: All right, let’s talk about it. Let’s get it in here and look at it.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Why are we wasting time? We all know what it looks like.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: You brought it up.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: The knife, and the way it was bought, is important evidence.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I agree.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Let’s establish the facts. The boy left home after being hit by his father. He went to a nearby shop and bought a switchblade. It had a very unusual carved handle. The shopkeeper said it was the only one of its kind he had ever had in stock.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Exactly!

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Three friends saw the knife that evening. Each identified it in court. The boy claims that must have fallen through a hole in his pocket on his way to the movies and he never saw it again.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: And then his father mysteriously ends up with it buried in his chest.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Exactly. Are you suggesting someone found the boy’s knife and then used it to murder his father?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: No. I’m saying it’s possible someone else stabbed his father with a similar knife.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Take a look at it. I’ve never seen one like it. Neither had the shopkeeper. A second knife would be an incredible coincidence.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’m just saying that it’s possible that there was a similar knife.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: And I’m saying it’s not possible.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Look at it! It’s the same knife.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Where’d that come from?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Where did you get that knife?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I walked through the boy’s neighbourhood last night. I bought it in a little shop three blocks from his house.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: It’s against the law to buy or sell switchblade knives.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s right. I broke the law. Arrest me.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Maybe there are ten knives like that. So what?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Maybe there are.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: It would still be an incredible coincidence for someone else to have stabbed the father with the same kind of knife.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: The odds are a million to one.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Exactly. It’s possible.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: But not very probable.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Maybe there are ten knives like that. So what does it prove?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Maybe nothing. But if the boy bought the knife to use on his father, why would he show the murder weapon to three friends just a couple of hours before the killing?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: And if he knew the knife could be identified, why would he leave it at the scene of the crime? He was bound to get arrested.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: He claims he bought it as a present for a friend. He dropped his friend’s knife and broke it.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: That’s true. The friend testified the boy broke his knife.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: The boy lied and you know it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: He may have lied.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Sure he lied.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you think he lied?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I… I’m not sure.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You’re not sure? What are you, the kid’s lawyer?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Isn’t that what’s supposed to happen in a jury room? A discussion of the facts? Aren’t we meant to be sure before we return the verdict?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: There are still eleven of us who think he’s guilty.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Look, you’re not gonna change anybody’s mind. Jesus, we could be here all night arguing about this!

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: It’s only one night. A boy may die.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Somebody saw the kid stab his father. What more do we need?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Okay. Let’s stay on track.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Look, I have a proposition. I’d like you eleven men to vote by secret ballot. I’ll abstain. If there are still eleven votes for guilty, we’ll take a guilty verdict into the judge right now. But if any one of you votes not guilty, we stay and talk it out.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Finally you’re behaving like a reasonable man.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right. Pass these along.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Guilty. Not guilty. Guilty.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: All right, who was it?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: This was a secret ballot. We agreed on that.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I know who it was. You come in here and vote guilty like everybody else, then this preacher starts telling stories about some poor little kid and you change your vote. You absolute –

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Now wait a minute. You can’t talk to me like that!

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: He didn’t change his vote. I did.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: This gentleman has been standing alone against us. He doesn’t say the boy is innocent. He just isn’t sure. It’s not easy to stand alone and be ridiculed. He gambled for support, and I gave it to him. The boy on trial is probably guilty. But I want to hear more.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right. That makes it ten to two.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Okay. Let’s get back to the old man downstairs. He heard the kid yell, ‘I’m going to kill you.’ A second later he heard the body hit the floor. Then he saw the kid run out of the house. What does that mean to you?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: How long does it take an elevated train to pass a given point?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Ten or twelve seconds.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: That sounds right.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Say ten seconds. What are you getting at?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: The tracks ran right past the boy’s window. I used to live next to an elevated line. When a train goes by, the noise is almost unbearable. You can’t hear yourself think.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Get to the point.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: The old man says he heard the boy shout, ‘I’m going to kill you,’ and a second later heard the body fall?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: That’s right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: And the woman across the street says she saw the killing through the last two cars of the passing train?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: So?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: If the train takes ten seconds to pass, it was roaring past the old man’s window for nearly ten seconds before the body fell. He would have had to hear the boy shout while the train was passing. How could he have heard him?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Of course he could have heard him. The old man said the boy yelled.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Even if he heard something over the noise of the train, how could he identify the voice?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You’re talking about a matter of seconds. Nobody can be that accurate.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Testimony that can send someone to the gallows should be that accurate.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I don’t think he could have heard it.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Neither do I. Not with the train going by.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Why would the old man lie? What’s he got to gain?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Attention, maybe.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Attention?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I watched him in court. A frightened old man in a torn jacket, dragging one leg. He’s spent his whole life being ignored. Nobody knows him. Nobody asks his advice. He’s… unimportant to society. Suddenly people are listening to every word he says.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: You think he’d lie just to feel important?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Not deliberately. But perhaps he convinced himself that he heard those words and recognised the boy.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: This case is based on facts.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Facts may be coloured by the people who present them.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Suppose the old man really did hear the boy say, ‘I’m going to kill you.’ How many times have we all used that phrase? ‘I could kill you for that.’ ‘If you do that once more, I’m going to kill you.’ We say it every day. It doesn’t mean we’re actually going to kill someone.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: The kid screamed it at the top of his lungs. Don’t tell me he didn’t mean it.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I don’t know. I’ve said things like that when I was angry.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: And would the boy really shout it so everyone in the vicinity could hear him?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: He’s a common, ignorant slob. He don’t even speak good English.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: He doesn’t even speak good English.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I’d like to change my vote to not guilty.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: You’ve got to be kidding.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: You heard me.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: That makes it nine to three for guilty.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Nine to three. He’s still guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: There’s something else about the old man. He said he heard the body fall, got out of bed and reached his front door in fifteen seconds, just in time to see the boy running downstairs.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: So?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: He was seventy-five years old. He dragged one leg when he walked. You said so yourself.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: They did have to help him into the witness chair…

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I want to see whether he could have reached that door in fifteen seconds.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You can’t recreate a thing like that.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: I’d like to see it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: His bed was twelve feet from the bedroom door. From there it was another forty-three feet to the front door. Make a sound for the body falling. Then I’ll start.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: This is ridiculous! He could have done it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Then let’s prove it.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I’ve got a watch.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: When I start, time me.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: This is ridiculous.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I’m walking faster than he did in court.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Much faster.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Come on! Get on with it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Stop. What’s the time?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Forty-two seconds.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Forty-two!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I think the old man heard the body fall. He got up, heard someone running downstairs and assumed it was the boy. But he couldn’t have reached his door in fifteen seconds.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: I think that’s possible.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What’s the matter with you people? You know this kid is guilty. He’s got to hang. We’re letting him slip through our fingers!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Slip through our fingers? Are you his executioner?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I’m one of ’em.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Maybe you’d like to put the noose around his neck.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: For this kid? You bet I would.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You want to see this boy die because you personally want it, not because of the facts.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Shut up!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You’re a sadist!

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Shut up! I’ll kill you! I’ll kill you!

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You don’t really mean you’ll kill me, do you?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: I think we should take another vote.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: An open vote. Let’s see who stands where.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All right. The last vote was eight to four for guilty. Number Two?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Not guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Three?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Four?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Five?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Not guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Six?

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Not guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Seven?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Eight?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Not guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Nine?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Not guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Ten?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Eleven?

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: Not guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Twelve?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: Six to six.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Six to six! Some of you people are out of your minds.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: The kind of boy he is has nothing to do with it. The facts are supposed to determine the case.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: What other facts? We’ve gone over this already.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: There’s still his alibi. He claimed he was at the cinema, but he couldn’t remember the name of the film or who was in it.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Let me ask you something. Where were you three nights ago?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: What?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Three nights ago. Where were you?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I went from court to my office, stayed there until eight-thirty, then went home.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: And the night before that?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I played bridge.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: And the night before that?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Monday. My wife and I went to the cinema.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What did you see?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I can’t remember the title of the film. Mrs — Mainbridge. No, Bainbridge.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I saw that one.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Who was in it?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Barbara — Long, I think.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Who else?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I don’t remember.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: And you weren’t under any emotional strain?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: I think the point is made.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: What point? That doesn’t prove the boy was at the cinema.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: No. But it means we can’t prove he wasn’t. He might have been there and forgotten what he saw.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: That is possible.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: So we’re still six to six.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: There’s something that’s been bothering me. The stab wound. The downward angle of it.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: They went over that in court.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I know. But the boy is five foot seven. His father was six foot two. Isn’t it awkward to stab down into the chest of someone seven inches taller than you?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Give me that knife. I’ll show you. Somebody get up.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Fine, I’ll do it. Let’s just get this over with.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I’m six or seven inches shorter than you. Right?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: Right.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: There’s your angle. Down and in. That’s how I’d stab a taller man in the chest. Now tell me I’m wrong. You don’t need any other evidence.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Down and in. I guess there’s no argument.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Wait a minute. Give me that. I hate these things. I grew up with them.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Have you seen them used in fights?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Too many times. You don’t use a switchblade that way. You hold it like this to release the blade. To stab downwards you’d have to change your grip.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: So how would you use it?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Underhand. Like this. Anyone who’s ever used a switchblade would never handle it any other way.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Are you sure?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: I’m sure.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Everyone agreed the boy was experienced with a knife.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: That’s right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Would he have made the kind of wound that killed his father?

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: Not with the experience he had. He’d go underhand.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: You can’t be certain what kind of wound he might have made just because he knew how to handle a knife.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Exactly.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: What do you think?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I don’t know.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What do you mean, you don’t know?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: I don’t know.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: I’m sick of this whole thing. All this talking is getting us nowhere. I’m changing my vote to not guilty.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You’re what?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: You heard me. I’ve had enough.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s no reason to change your vote!

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: He’s right. That is not a reason. You have sat here and voted guilty because you wanted to get to a baseball game. Now you change your vote because you’re tired of talking. What kind of a man are you?

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: I don’t have to explain myself.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: You do have to. A man’s life is at stake. Say why.

script.speaker: 7th Juror
script.text: I don’t think he’s guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Mr Foreman, another vote?

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: All those voting not guilty, raise your hands.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I don’t understand you people. All these picky little points don’t mean anything. How can you believe his story? You know what they’re like.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: What do you mean, ‘they’?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: You know exactly what I mean. People like this boy. A kid from the slums. They don’t need any big excuse to kill someone. Everybody knows it. They’re violent. Human life doesn’t mean as much to them as it does to us.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Do you know you’re a sick man?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Sick?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Why don’t you sit down and keep your sanctimonious opinions to yourself?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Who the hell are you to say that to me? I’m speaking my piece and you’re going to listen. These people are fighting all the time. If somebody gets killed, so somebody gets killed. They don’t care. Family doesn’t mean anything to them.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Maybe if you just quietened down –

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I will like hell quiet down. We’re facing a danger here. These people are multiplying. That kid on trial — his type — they’re wild animals. They’re against us. They hate us.

script.speaker: 6th Juror
script.text: Ah, shut up!

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: I’m warning you. This boy — we’ve got him. That’s one at least we can deal with. I say get him before his kind gets us. I don’t give a damn about the law. Why should I? They don’t.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: I’ve heard enough. Stop it.

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: How would you like me to cave your head in?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: We’ve heard enough. Sit down. And don’t open your filthy mouth again.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It’s very hard to keep personal prejudice out of a thing like this. Prejudice obscures the truth. Nine of us now have a reasonable doubt. We may be wrong and we’d be returning a guilty man to the community. No one can really know. But no jury can declare a man guilty unless they’re certain. Now, we can’t understand how you three are still so sure. Maybe you can tell us.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Okay… I still believe the boy is guilty because of the woman across the street. She actually saw the murder.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s the most important testimony in the whole case.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: She went to bed at about eleven. Her bed was next to the window, directly opposite the boy’s room. At ten past twelve she looked out and saw the killing through the windows of the passing train. She says she got a good look at the boy stabbing his father. As far as I can see, that testimony is unshakeable.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: That’s the whole case. Irrefutable evidence beyond reasonable doubt.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Are you all right?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I’m perfectly well.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: You were rubbing your nose.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: It bothers me a little.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Because of your glasses?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Yes. Can we get on?

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Your glasses make deep impressions on the sides of your nose.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: They do.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: The woman who testified had those same marks.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s right! She kept rubbing them in court.

script.speaker: 5th Juror
script.text: She did.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: You don’t know she wore glasses.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: I saw the marks too. I was closest to her.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: Could those marks be made by anything other than glasses?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: So she wore glasses. So what? She was at home when she saw the murder.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you wear your glasses in bed?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No. Nobody wears glasses to bed.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: She was lying in bed trying to sleep. It’s reasonable to suppose she wasn’t wearing them.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: How do you know?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I don’t. I’m guessing. But she probably didn’t have time to put them on. Maybe she honestly thought she saw the boy kill his father. Maybe she saw only a blur.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Maybe she was farsighted. What do you know about it?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: I know her eyesight is now in question.

script.speaker: 11th Juror
script.text: She had to identify someone sixty feet away, in the dark, without her glasses.

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: You can’t send someone to die on evidence like that.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Don’t you think she might have made a mistake?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: No.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It’s not possible?

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: No. It’s not possible.

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Could it be possible?

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: You mean, is it possible the woman made a mistake?

script.speaker: 12th Juror
script.text: Yes. I say not guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Do you still think he’s guilty?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Yes, I think he’s guilty. But I couldn’t care less anymore.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: How do you vote?

script.speaker: 10th Juror
script.text: Not guilty. Do whatever you want.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I think he’s guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Does anyone else think he’s guilty?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: No. I’m convinced.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What’s the matter with you?

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: I now have a reasonable doubt.

script.speaker: 9th Juror
script.text: It’s eleven to one.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What about all the other evidence? The knife — the whole business?

script.speaker: 2nd Juror
script.text: You said we could throw out all the other evidence.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: Face it. You’re alone.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I don’t care whether I’m alone or not. It’s my right.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: It’s your right.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Well, what do you want? I say he’s guilty.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: We want your arguments.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: I gave you my arguments.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: We’re not convinced. We want to hear them again. We have as much time as it takes.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: Fine, you want to hear my arguments? You want the truth? Everything that came out in that courtroom says he’s guilty. Do you think I’m an idiot? You’re not going to intimidate me into silence. I’m entitled to my opinion.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: That’s true.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: What about the old man? He heard everything. He saw the boy on the stairs. What difference does it make how many seconds it took? And the knife. Just because you found another one like it doesn’t prove anything. Everything that went on has been twisted and turned in here. The woman testified in court. How do you know she didn’t have her glasses on? And the old man heard the boy yell, ‘I’m going to kill you.’ That’s what he said. To his own father. I don’t care what kind of a man he was. He was his father. My God, don’t you see? How come I’m the only one who sees? I can feel that knife going in. That rotten kid. I know him. I know what boys are like. What they do to you. How they kill you every day.

script.speaker: 8th Juror
script.text: But it’s not your boy. He’s somebody else.

script.speaker: 4th Juror
script.text: Let him live.

script.speaker: 3rd Juror
script.text: All right. Not guilty.

script.speaker: Foreman
script.text: We’re ready.

script.speaker: Guard
script.text: All right, gentlemen. Gather your things and come along.
